[Interview, 2005-05-27, News & Notes]
HOST: ...and didn't have sleep before, that night.
GUEST: I thought, `Man!' You know, I could understand. I could understand his point of view, based on what teachers told me a long time ago.

HOST: Dawn?

HOST: Sure.

HOST: What of the thought, though, here that there is--and maybe we're missing the bigger picture here. There is a sense, an environment in many schools, that this is what goes on, on an everyday basis--the occurrence of unruly students, the occurrence of an inability to truly set an environment that's conducive to learning. You know, we laugh at this and we feel bad for this teacher, but the reality is this is more typical than we'd like to believe.
GUEST: Well, you know, we discussed on here...

HOST: Unless you can't spell.
GUEST: Unless you can't spell--right. And, you know, he was trying to do a fun thing for the kids, and he was like, `They're just so unruly, they mess up everything.'

HOST: Yeah. Yeah.

HOST: Since we're telling the truth, I was one of those kids who took the early seat. `The: T--oh, shoot.'

HOST: Go ahead, Dawn.

HOST: Right.

HOST: Yeah. I think that we talk a lot when we talk about, you know, that children are our future, our most precious resources, but I think that's a lot of--well, you know what I think it's a lot of.
GUEST: Baloney. Baloney. Baloney. Baloney.

HOST: Baloney.

HOST: Because there are tremendous problems going on in our schools, not just in behavior but, as we've talked about before, lack of books, lack of opportunity, lack of everything that one needs to have a formal education. And it's difficult. I think we really have to start looking at that.

HOST: All right. Enough of my preaching. GUEST, Dawn Turner Trice and George Curry, thank you all for being with us today. Enjoy your holiday.

HOST: George...

HOST: Not too much eating, man. Be careful.

HOST: All right.

[Interview, 2005-07-12, News & Notes]
HOST: OK. There you go.

HOST: Right.

HOST: Right.

[Interview, 2005-08-12, News & Notes]
HOST: E.R., if I hear from you...

HOST: ...you're suggesting there's nothing that he can say.

HOST: Well, no, but if we--let's assume we're allowing her to be the collective face of those grieving, he can...

HOST: ...in turn, turn it around and suggest that he meets with her symbolically as the collective face of those who are grieving.

HOST: Yeah. All right.

HOST: Right, but...

HOST: Now you...

HOST: Yeah.

HOST: Yeah.

HOST: Obviously, it remains...

HOST: It remains...

HOST: All right.
GUEST: That's true.

[Interview, 2005-08-30, News & Notes]
HOST: All right. We'll turn our attention now to the CIA. And an independent watchdog organization has represented--or recommended, I should say, that disciplinary reviews for current and former officials who were involved in the failed intelligence efforts before the attack on 9/11 should, in fact take place. It was harshly critical of many senior officials, including former CIA Director George Tenet. The irony here is that current CIA Director Porter Goss must now decide whether disciplinary proceedings will go forward. A, Renee, do you believe that, in fact, we should continue to dig into this and hold people accountable? Some will suggest that this is one of those things that you cannot prevent.

HOST: Well, yeah. I mean, let's use the key word, which is `accountability.' Who does the buck ultimately stop with, and how do we even say that it's acceptable to set a precedent where, if this kind of information was known prior to an attack, that it's justifiable on any level and that someone should be held accountable, even if it's through a letter; someone should be held accountable, even if it's through the form of disciplinary action. And I think, GUEST, as you mentioned, we really are talking about just putting these people up before investigation. It may come out that they would be exonerated. But the point is, let's push towards accountability. If we're challenging other folks in corporate America to be accountable, if we're challenging people, even our young people, to be accountable through their education, ultimately, the federal government should be held to a as high, if not higher, standard of accountability.

HOST: Absolutely. And, again, I think that, if it's possible, if there is real information and there was real errors made on the part of people at highest levels, that those people should be held accountable for those errors. If those errors did not take place, then so be it. But I do not believe that we have the luxury of allowing people in positions with this amount of authority, that have the ability to affect so many lives, not to be held accountable or at least not create the procedures that ensure that the maximum level of accountability is reached.

HOST: And sometimes it's really--in my mind, it's just about having a level of integrity to the process. Even at the end of it, if you don't get to the result that everyone wanted, you can at least say that you pushed for the highest level of accountability possible, and that's my issue. I think that's the standard that we need to set.

HOST: And, GUEST, isn't, to a great degree, perhaps that the most important aspect of all of this--the idea of bringing back a level of trust, as best you can have it, with operatives like those in the CIA and FBI and the like? There has been a sense of mystery removed from this community, and perhaps, like "The Wizard of Oz," us looking at this community and feeling that maybe you weren't as smart as we thought.
GUEST: Or maybe you were as dumb as we always thought. I don't know which that is. But I think that, yeah, like--I think it's important to hold this--to hold everybody--you know, make sure that they did what they did, and if they didn't, they have to, you know, be accountable for that. So, you know, it--I think it would help the families, honestly, and I think it would help the American public just to see it, but also agree that eventually you have to just let this--you have to let the new system work.

HOST: Yeah.
GUEST: You have to see how it works.

HOST: Yeah.

[Interview, 2006-11-01, News & Notes]
HOST: Okay.

HOST: Yeah.

[Interview, 2007-01-30, News & Notes]
HOST: Well…

h6_poor_b1000.block:
[Interview, 2007-02-28, News & Notes]
HOST: Thanks everybody.

[Interview, 2007-03-06, News & Notes]
HOST: GUEST, he is, in some ways, the candidate who has been most clear about what he's going to campaign on. He's campaigning on this labor and two Americas issue, whereas Barack Obama and Hillary Clinton have talked about a multitude of issues. Is it smart for Edwards to be focused so much so early?
GUEST: You know, I'm not really certain if it's - I guess - because, you know, we have to remember, we're almost still two years away from this election. A lot can change in this time. Right now, I don't really know if people are going to necessarily remember what he's talking about. I don't know if they're going to remember in November of 2008, what he's talking - or even a year from now what he's talking about right now. So sure, he can focus on various issues, and perhaps he's trying to talk about these issues because right now, maybe, most people probably still associate him with John Kerry who was, of course, from, you know, wore his upper crust right out front. So Edwards is trying to connect with the people. And really, he's got the - I guess, he's got the cache to do it. Because he's sort of the forgotten kid right now, and I say kid just because he used kind of youthful looking. But he's really got a great story, he's - you know, a former senator, lawyer from his bootstraps type of thing. His wife - he stood by her as she had cancer. So he's got a lot going for him that, you know, he just kind of stays of the course, it might began to resonate more and more as he gets well - more well known.

HOST: So, Michael, he started his campaign in New Orleans dealing with the issues of Katrina survivors. Again, does this really carry him forward as a candidate?

HOST: Okay. Well, we'll have to keep an eye on that. I just want to reintroduce everybody. In case you're just tuning in, this is NPR's NEWS & NOTES. I'm Farai Chideya. You were just listening to the inimitable Michael Meyers, executive director of the New York Civil Rights Coalition. We've got Laura Washington, Chicago Sun-Times Columnist, GUEST, staff writer for People Magazine. Moving on to Cherokees and black descendants in the tribe.

HOST: So, over the weekend, the Cherokee Nation members decided to revoke the tribal citizenship of about 2,800 descendants of slaves who were owned by Cherokees. Over 75 percent of nation members voted in favor of an amendment to the tribal constitution that would limit citizenship to tribe members that are descendants by blood.

HOST: Now this is an issue that has not just been limited to the Cherokee Nation but Seminoles have had controversies over whether or not black Seminoles, and there are many, are given the same rights as other Seminoles. What do we make of this? Because in America, Native Americans have kind of a dual citizenship status almost, where you have people who are citizens of America but also citizens of their own tribal nations.

HOST: And there were people who were either owned as slaves by different native nations or who were intermixed and intermarried. So does this sound like racism to, at this point in time in the 21st century, decide to kick people out? Laura?

HOST: Michael?

HOST: It's more that so many tribes do have these odd mixtures, and at this point is it fair to separate people out?
GUEST: Well, you know, I mean you're right. Who among us is pure, so to speak? Is it fair? You know, I kind of look at this in the, you know, thinking of the Cherokee dilemmas. I mean, no people in this country have been more marginalized or disenfranchised, or cheated or downtrodden than the Native Americans of this country. And it's sort of like, you know, they have that 1866 treaty that assured the (unintelligible) their descendants that they will be, you know, part of the tribe. It took them 141 years to break that treaty. They wish the white man had taken that long to break the treaties they wrote with them. I really don't feel so uptight about this because, as Laura pointed out, these people were almost exterminated. You know, they were almost exterminated - they almost don't even exist. They are the original people in this country, at least for the last 700 years or whatever, and they're like the smallest group here because they almost didn't even exist anymore. So I really don't have any problem with them trying to hold on to something that may have never really existed, but they're trying to hold on to it now and stay sort of who they are. And, you know, if black people sort of have to, quote-unquote, "suffer" at that, I really don't have that big a qualm, big issue with it.

HOST: All right. Well, let me make a small correction. It's the Foxwoods Resorts that the Pequot tribe owns. But I think we've done with this story…

HOST: We have two minutes left, so I have a speed round for you. It's about pep, and what kind of pep do you have based on race? In California, a high school called Mt. Diablo High School divided students by ethnicity and featured jazz music for black students, flags from Asian countries for Asian students. They had white students' rallies and Hispanic students' rallies.

HOST: Laura, we're almost out of time.

HOST: All right. Well…

HOST: Okay. On that note, got to wrap it up. Laura Washington, columnist for the Chicago Sun-Times, GUEST, staff writer for People magazine, and Michael Meyers, executive director of the New York Civil Rights Coalition. Thank you all.

HOST: And next on NEWS & NOTES, you down with OPP? Well, the new book "Other People's Property" breaks down why rap is music to white ears. And Haiti and Ghana, two countries with one goal of independence. How they each won their freedom.
